burnham-patriot-missiles-lobbying.headline: Burnham to press Trump for Patriot missiles before Russia's winter strikes
burnham-patriot-missiles-lobbying.body_md:
The train that carried Andy Burnham into Kyiv on Monday morning was, in a narrow sense, just the latest stop on a well-worn diplomatic circuit — Western leaders marking Ukraine's independence day, reaffirming solidarity, posing for photographs with President Volodymyr Zelenskyy against a backdrop of sandbagged monuments. But for Britain's still-new prime minister, it was something more specific: his first foreign trip since taking office, and the start of a lobbying campaign aimed squarely at Washington.

Burnham's message in Kyiv was blunt enough. Ukraine is running out of Patriot interceptors — the one weapon in its arsenal that can reliably bring down Russian ballistic missiles — just as Moscow prepares to repeat, and likely intensify, last winter's campaign against the country's power grid. Having heard that appeal in person from Zelenskyy, Burnham now says he intends to carry it to Donald Trump.

![UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/67/Prime_Minister_Andy_Burnham_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg)

"I've not fully confirmed the details yet, but it's likely I will go, particularly after today's discussion," Burnham told Bloomberg in Kyiv on Monday evening. "Leaving today, I'm quite clear what I need to do in the next few weeks." He is expected to travel to New York next month for the UN General Assembly, where he and other European leaders are weighing a fresh gathering of the so-called Coalition of the Willing timed to catch Trump in the same city — and, they hope, in a receptive mood.

## A shortage with a number attached

The scale of the problem is not abstract. Ukraine has received roughly 600 Patriot interceptors over the course of the war, according to figures cited by a Zelenskyy adviser, and has expended nearly all of them. Zelenskyy is now asking for an emergency package of 300 more before the cold sets in — enough, Ukrainian officials argue, to plug the gap left as Russia's missile production has outpaced what Kyiv can shoot down. On 6 July, by one account, Ukraine failed to intercept a single ballistic missile fired at it, the first day of the war that happened.

The difficulty is supply. Current estimates put total US Patriot interceptor stocks at somewhere between 759 and 827 missiles — roughly a third of what the Pentagon held before American and Israeli strikes on Iran earlier this year diverted stock toward US bases and regional allies in the Middle East. Handing Ukraine the 300 interceptors Zelenskyy wants would, on those figures, cut what remains in American warehouses by close to half. That is the trade-off Trump will be asked to weigh, and it explains why the administration has so far offered warm words rather than commitments: at a recent meeting with Zelenskyy, Trump said the missiles were "very hard to get" but that "we are going to see if we can make some of them available."

![Patriot air-defense missile launcher](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/8a/German_Patriot_missile_launcher.jpg)

Ukraine's own build-out of energy defences is a hedge, not a substitute. Kyiv has spent the year distributing power generation into smaller, harder-to-target sources and shoring up substations after last winter's bombardment knocked out roughly 80% of the country's generation capacity at points and left a six-gigawatt shortfall, according to First Deputy Prime Minister Denys Shmyhal. Repair bills from that campaign alone have been estimated at $64–70 billion. None of that changes the fact that only Patriot batteries can reliably stop the ballistic missiles Russia aims at the grid — and that Moscow, by Western intelligence assessments, is already massing for a renewed strike campaign against Kyiv's energy infrastructure in the coming weeks, backed by a sharply expanded drone programme.

## Kyiv, then the wider coalition

Burnham's visit was not a solo affair. He met Zelenskyy alongside a cluster of European figures marking Ukraine's 35th independence anniversary — European Council President António Costa, Moldovan President Maia Sandu, Luxembourg's Prime Minister Luc Frieden, Estonian President Alar Karis and Nordic and Baltic leaders among them — with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron joining by video link to co-chair a session of the Coalition of the Willing. The UK used the trip to announce that defence contractor MBDA would be permitted to share classified technical information on the Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missile with Ukraine, a step toward local assembly lines rather than continued reliance on shipments from abroad.

That detail matters for reading the Patriot request correctly. European governments are simultaneously trying to help Ukraine build more of its own capability and trying to unlock the one category of weapon — long-range interceptors — that only the United States can supply at scale. The Kremlin, for its part, has cast the diplomacy as evidence that the West wants the war prolonged rather than ended. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said this week that "such escalatory statements have prevailed... they want the war to continue," a framing Moscow has used before to characterise Western air-defence support as an obstacle to negotiation rather than a defensive necessity.

## Why this is still theatre, for now

What Burnham secured in Kyiv was attention, not interceptors. No release of additional Patriot stock has been confirmed by the Trump administration, and the arithmetic of America's own depleted stockpile means any decision will be contested inside the Pentagon regardless of what Trump tells European visitors in New York. Burnham's trip is best read as one node in a wider European effort — alongside Merz, Macron and the Coalition of the Willing — to keep Washington's attention on Ukraine's air defences before Trump faces the domestic pressure that has, at various points, pushed his administration toward scaling back aid.

The test of whether this amounts to more than diplomatic choreography will come at the UN General Assembly session in New York next month, where Burnham hopes for a face-to-face opening with Trump. Russia, meanwhile, is not waiting on the outcome: the strike campaign Ukrainian and Western officials expect against the power grid could begin before that meeting even takes place.

lottery-boss-scrutiny.headline: National Lottery's incoming boss faces scrutiny over gambling-industry background
lottery-boss-scrutiny.body_md:
Britain's National Lottery has spent three decades selling itself as a harmless flutter — the £2 ticket that funds village halls and Olympic swimmers, kept carefully apart in the public mind from the slot machines and betting apps that make up the rest of the gambling industry. That distinction is now under strain, after the operator handed interim control of the £6.5bn, ten-year licence to a former bookmaking executive with a disciplinary record from the regulator that oversees him.

Allwyn UK confirmed on 19 August that Phil Walker, who spent six years at William Hill including stints as UK & Ireland managing director and chief commercial officer, will take over as interim chief executive from 7 September, replacing Andria Vidler while a permanent successor is sought. Vidler, who steered the National Lottery's licence transition from Camelot and a subsequent digital overhaul, stays on in an advisory capacity until the end of October.

![UK National Lottery ticket dispensers inside a Tesco Extra superstore in Poole, Dorset](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/1b/UK_National_Lottery_ticket_dispensers_inside_Tesco_Extra_superstore%2C_Tower_Park%2C_Poole%2C_Dorset%2C_England.jpg)

## A regulator's own sanction, now under his old employer's roof

The appointment has drawn a formal challenge from Parliament. Labour's Dawn Butler and Conservative Iain Duncan Smith have written to the Gambling Commission saying they are "deeply concerned" by the choice, pointing to a personal sanction the Commission imposed on Walker in 2024 over what it called "widespread and alarming" failures to enforce anti-money-laundering and terrorist-financing controls during his time at William Hill. The firm was fined a record £19.2m in March 2023 across three group entities, after failures that let at least one customer gamble £23,000 in minutes without any checks. The MPs have asked the regulator to explain what weight, if any, it gave that history when Allwyn assessed Walker's fitness for a role overseeing the country's only legal lottery monopoly.

A second thread compounds the concern: Walker sits on the board of Game Nation, Britain's third-largest chain of adult gaming centres, for a role reportedly worth over £50,000 a year. He has agreed to step back from it from 1 September for the duration of his interim contract — a concession MPs are treating as confirmation the conflict was real rather than incidental.

Allwyn's defence is narrow but pointed: the Gambling Commission did not strip Walker of his personal operating licence over the William Hill failings, which it takes as evidence the regulator already judged him fit to work in the sector. The Commission itself has declined to comment publicly, citing a policy of not discussing operators' personnel decisions — leaving the question of oversight resting, for now, on Allwyn's own judgment rather than the regulator's.

## What comes next

The episode lands as the National Lottery already faces broader scrutiny of its public-interest obligations under Allwyn's licence, and as MPs continue pressing the Gambling Commission for a substantive reply. The next marker will be whether that letter produces one, and who Allwyn names as Walker's permanent successor once the search concludes.

hormuz-mines-cleared.headline: US Navy clears Strait of Hormuz of mines as Trump warns Iran off new deployments
hormuz-mines-cleared.body_md:
The Strait of Hormuz has been the fault line running through the global oil market for most of this year. On Tuesday, President Trump said the fault has been sealed shut — for now.

"I have just been informed by the United States Navy that all mines have been removed and/or detonated from within the International Waters of the Strait of Hormuz," Trump wrote on Truth Social. He paired the announcement with a warning: any vessel caught laying new mines would be "immediately and systematically destroyed," and the U.S. Space Force would now watch "every square inch" of the strait under what he called a "Zero Tolerance policy."

It is the clearest sign yet that Washington considers the acute phase of a conflict that began in February — when U.S. and Israeli strikes on Iran triggered a retaliation campaign across the Gulf — to be over, even as the diplomatic and economic fight with Tehran enters a new phase.

## How the strait got mined

Hormuz carries about a fifth of the world's seaborne oil and a comparable share of its liquefied natural gas, funneled through a channel barely two miles wide at its narrowest shipping lanes. When Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps began laying mines there in March, in response to the U.S.-Israeli campaign, the effect on markets was immediate: Brent crude, which had been trading in the $70s, jumped to around $100 a barrel within days, and briefly threatened $150 as fighting intensified through the spring.

![USS Essex and USNS Wally Schirra transit the Strait of Hormuz in formation](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/b/b6/USS_Essex_%28LHD_2%29%2C_right%2C_and_USNS_Wally_Schirra_%28T-AKE_8%29_transit_the_Strait_of_Hormuz_in_formation._%2851531961733%29.jpg)

U.S. Central Command opened a mine-clearance operation in April, deploying destroyers, mine countermeasures ships and unmanned underwater drones to sweep the channel and re-establish safe transit corridors. It has taken four months. OPEC+ tried to blunt the price shock in the interim by raising output quotas — a modest 206,000 barrels a day from May — but the real ceiling on prices was always going to be set by whether tankers could move through Hormuz without hitting a mine, not by how much crude Gulf producers were willing to pump.

## The premium comes out

The market's answer arrived in real time this week. The Murban crude premium to Brent — a proxy for how much extra insurance traders demand for oil that has to physically pass through Hormuz — stood above $11 a barrel on Monday and had roughly halved by Tuesday afternoon as word of the clearance spread. Brent itself settled near $87 on Tuesday, down for a second straight session, as what traders had been calling the "war premium" continued to unwind.

That is still well above the pre-crisis baseline in the $70s, and a long way from the triple-digit spikes of March and April. But the direction is the point: a persistent, months-long tail risk that had been priced into every barrel of Gulf crude is being repriced downward, barrel by barrel, as the physical threat recedes. For a global economy still nursing above-target inflation, one fewer supply shock vector running through energy markets is a genuine, if modest, disinflationary data point.

## The threat hasn't fully gone quiet

Trump's announcement did not mean the Gulf has gone calm. Hours before the mine-clearance statement, an oil tanker was struck by an unidentified projectile roughly nine nautical miles off Oman's coast, disabling its engine room; the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency, which tracks such incidents, said it could not identify who fired it. It was the latest in a string of projectile strikes on commercial vessels near the strait that have continued even as the mine threat has been cleared, underscoring that demining removes one hazard to shipping, not all of them.

The timing also coincided with a sharp escalation on the sanctions front. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent unveiled what the administration is calling "Operation Economic Outcast," targeting nearly 60 individuals, entities and vessels and opening five sectors of Iran's economy — digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping — to broader secondary sanctions. "We are launching an economic onslaught against Iran's financial connections around the globe," Bessent said, adding that any entity found laundering money on Iran's behalf would be cut off from the U.S. dollar system.

China, Iran's largest trading partner and the top buyer of its oil, condemned the move within hours. Foreign ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said Beijing opposed "illegal, unilateral" sanctions and warned the measures would "only further intensify tensions" — a reminder that Washington's demining announcement and its sanctions expansion are two halves of the same strategy: physically secure the strait while squeezing Tehran's revenue everywhere else.

## What the clearance actually changes

For energy markets, the practical effect is straightforward: insurers, shippers and refiners no longer have to price in a live minefield across the world's most important chokepoint. That lowers the floor under freight and war-risk premiums that had been added to every Gulf cargo since March, and it removes one of the clearer arguments for crude staying persistently elevated regardless of what OPEC+ does with quotas.

What it does not do is resolve the underlying standoff. Iran has not accepted the sanctions escalation quietly, and the projectile strike off Oman shows the campaign against shipping has other tools besides mines. Trump's "zero tolerance" language is as much a deterrent bet as a victory lap — it commits the U.S. to treating any future mining as an act warranting immediate retaliation, which raises the stakes of the next incident even as it lowers the odds, in the administration's telling, that one occurs.

The next test is less likely to be military than economic: whether China, still buying the bulk of Iran's oil exports, alters that behavior under the threat of secondary sanctions, and whether Brent's slide toward its pre-crisis range holds if it doesn't. Markets will be watching the Murban-Brent spread for the rest of the week as the more reliable gauge of whether Hormuz is actually calm, or just quiet.

labour-voting-reform-push.headline: Labour MPs push Burnham to back voting reform within first 100 days
labour-voting-reform-push.body_md:
The test of any new prime minister is not what he promises in the glow of victory, but what he does when his own backbenches start pushing. Andy Burnham, a little over five weeks into Downing Street, is about to find out.

When parliament returns from recess, an amendment tabled by the Leeds North West MP Alex Sobel will come back to the Commons floor on 2 September. It calls for a national commission to review Britain's first-past-the-post voting system — and it already carries 185 signatures from MPs across eight parties, 98 of them Labour. That is more support than any other amendment currently before parliament, according to figures reported by the Guardian, and a YouGov poll of MPs found 53% back some form of review of the electoral system.

![Prime Minister Andy Burnham's official portrait, taken at 10 Downing Street](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/67/Prime_Minister_Andy_Burnham_portrait_%28cropped%29.jpg)

> "Now we know a majority of MPs back this proposal... I know the prime minister is committed to reforming our electoral system." — Alex Sobel

## An awkward inheritance

Burnham arrives at this fight with an unusually clean paper trail. He is the first prime minister in modern British history to have openly backed proportional representation before taking office, a position he traces to his years running Greater Manchester under the Supplementary Vote system — an experience he has described as the moment that converted him from adversarial Westminster politics to something more consensual. At Labour's 2022 conference, as a backbench voice rather than a leader, he endorsed a manifesto commitment to PR for the next parliament.

That history is precisely why his MPs think they have leverage now. Rachel Blake, a former Treasury minister who backs the amendment, put it plainly: "The PLP agrees with Andy Burnham that first past the post is broken, and that a national commission is the way to get a grip on it." Lizzi Collinge, another signatory, framed the case in terms of fairness rather than party advantage, arguing that first-past-the-post "particularly devalues the votes of renters, young people and BAME people."

The MPs want more than warm words. They are asking Burnham to announce the commission before the autumn budget in October, with a mandate to report back ahead of the next general election — squarely inside the informal 100-day window by which a new government's seriousness is often judged.

## Number 10's caution

Downing Street has not said no. But it has not said yes either. Burnham's office describes him as "strongly committed to electoral reform" while stopping short of endorsing Sobel's specific commission, treating the question instead as one for Labour's next manifesto — a decision, in other words, that requires a fresh mandate rather than an executive order five weeks into a term nobody voted for on this basis.

The hesitation is not hard to explain. Reforming the system that delivered a government its majority always invites the charge of a stitch-up, particularly with Reform UK's rise reshaping the electoral map that first-past-the-post is meant to referee. Some of the amendment's most notable signatures — Miatta Fahnbulleh, Florence Eshalomi and Jo Platt, all now serving as ministers — may yet be withdrawn under the convention that frontbenchers do not sign backbench amendments, a quiet reminder of how differently the calculation looks once an MP has a government job to protect.

## Why this matters beyond the amendment

The vote itself is unlikely to bind the government to anything; amendments of this kind are more often a pressure gauge than a legislative event. What it measures is whether Burnham can hold the space between the reformist instincts that got him elected leader and the institutional caution that comes with actually running the country — and whether his backbenchers, flush with the size of their coalition, are willing to test that gap publicly this early.

A prime minister who spent years outside Westminster arguing that its voting system was broken now has to decide whether fixing it is worth spending political capital on before he has banked any wins. The 2 September vote will not settle the argument. But it will show, within his first weeks in office, whether Burnham leads his party on this question or is led by it.

uk-drone-factory-threat.headline: Former Russian minister warns UK drone factories could face attacks from 'unknown sources'
uk-drone-factory-threat.body_md:
A former Russian deputy foreign minister has raised the prospect of attacks on British factories that build drones for Ukraine — though he was careful, several times over, not to say who might carry them out.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, Andrei Fedorov, who now advises the Kremlin and directs a Moscow political research foundation, said he could not "exclude 100 percent that there might be some 'semi-military' action against Britain." Pressed on what that might look like, he offered: "something might happen with enterprises, with the factories which are producing drones for Ukraine." He mentioned hacking too — carried out, he said, by "unknown source, not official level, of course" — and vaguer "political steps." Asked directly whether Russia itself would strike, he said no: any attack would come "not by Russia, but from unknown sources."

It is a carefully hedged form of threat — deniable by design, attributable to no one, and delivered by a man who left government office years ago. That does not make it noise. It lands amid a broader pattern of sabotage and hybrid attacks that MI5's director general, Ken McCallum, has already linked to Russian state intent, and at a moment when Britain's drone industry has just become considerably harder for Moscow to ignore.

## The trigger

The remarks followed Prime Minister Andy Burnham's announcement in Kyiv this week that Britain would declassify blueprints for UK-made components of the Scalp missile — the French-built cousin of Storm Shadow — clearing the way for Ukraine to manufacture the long-range cruise missile domestically. Scalp variants have already been used to strike military and industrial sites deep inside Russia; handing over the technology to build them locally is a significant escalation in the UK's material support for Kyiv.

![Storm Shadow/SCALP cruise missile on display at the RAF Museum, London](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6d/Storm_Shadow-SCALP-EG_long-range_general-purpose_cruise_missile%2C_RAF_Museum%2C_London%2C_Ank_Kumar_%2C_Infosys_02.jpg)

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov followed with his own complaint, saying the UK was "participating in this war" and adding "fuel to the fire." Burnham's reply, when asked about it by reporters, was blunt: "Who started the fire? That's the question, isn't it?" — a pointed reference to Russia's 2022 invasion.

## A factory sector with something to lose

The warning targets an industry that barely existed at this scale two years ago. Under a £752 million contract announced in April, three British manufacturers — Tekever, Windracers and Malloy Aeronautics — are committed to supplying at least 120,000 drones to Ukraine by the end of 2026, the largest single-nation UAV commitment of the war. Tekever alone is opening a fourth UK site, a large facility in Swindon expected to create around 1,000 jobs, alongside expansion in Suffolk. The government has pitched the build-out explicitly as dual-purpose: supporting Ukraine while establishing Britain as a European centre of drone manufacturing.

That is precisely what makes the factories a plausible symbolic target, and precisely why Fedorov's comments, however vague, were picked up rather than shrugged off. Sites tied to war supply chains have already featured in the pattern of sabotage attributed to Russian intelligence networks across Europe — arson at a Warsaw shopping centre, damage to undersea cables in the Baltic — which McCallum has described as an effort to generate "sustained mayhem" on British and European streets using operatives who are not, on paper, Russian state actors. That precedent is what gives "unknown sources" its edge: it is the exact operating model security officials say Moscow already uses.

## What isn't there

What the warning does not contain is anything close to specifics. No factory was named, no timeframe given, no method beyond a shrugged-off mention of hacking. Fedorov is a private adviser now, not a serving official with operational knowledge, and his framing — "sooner or later, there might be not only verbal but maybe some visible reaction" — reads as an attempt to signal resolve to a domestic audience as much as a warning to London. Russian state media and commentators have been pushing Putin to respond more forcefully to Western arms support, and Fedorov himself has previously been willing to publicly needle the Kremlin's own conduct of the war. Rhetoric of this kind serves a purpose in Moscow independent of whether anything follows it.

None of that rules out the risk. It simply means investors and manufacturers are being asked to weigh a real vulnerability — under-defended commercial sites now central to a NATO ally's military supply chain — against a threat with no operational content attached to it yet.

The next marker to watch is less rhetorical: whether the UK's National Protective Security Authority updates guidance for defence contractors, and whether Tekever, Windracers or Malloy disclose any change to site security as their new facilities come online later this year.

twitch-ai-training-lawsuit.headline: Twitch and Amazon sued by streamers over undisclosed AI training on livestreams
twitch-ai-training-lawsuit.body_md:
Warren Pandiscia streams from Connecticut, the kind of small-to-mid Twitch creator whose channel keeps the platform's lights on without ever making him famous. Now he is the named plaintiff in a class action that asks a blunt question: when a platform quietly starts feeding your broadcasts into an AI training pipeline, who owns what comes out the other side?

The suit, filed August 20 in the US District Court for the Northern District of California, targets Twitch and its owner, Amazon. It alleges the companies used millions of streamers' livestreams, clips, video-on-demand uploads and chat logs to train generative AI models without licensing the content or paying for it — and, Pandiscia claims, without meaningfully asking first.

## A default nobody chose

The mechanics are the heart of the complaint. On August 12, Twitch rolled out a setting called "Training for Generative AI," tucked into the Security and Privacy tab of account settings. It was switched on for every creator by default. There was no email, no pop-up, no advance notice — streamers found out largely because word spread on social media and gaming press picked it up.

![Twitch logo](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/3f/Twitch_Logo.jpg)

Asked on a company livestream why the setting wasn't opt-in, Twitch's chief product officer Mike Minton gave an answer that has since become the case's most-quoted line: "If it was opt-in, nobody would opt in." Under public pressure, Twitch added an opt-out option days later. But the complaint argues the fix is cosmetic. The toggle only covers a streamer's own channel — anyone who chats on someone else's stream is still captured under that channel owner's settings, regardless of their personal preference. Pandiscia's filing puts it plainly: the systems are "incapable of obtaining" consent from everyone whose voice, image or words end up in a captured broadcast.

The complaint also alleges the scraping predates the disclosure by some margin, claiming Twitch and Amazon have been drawing on creator content for AI training since at least 2024.

## The claims and what's being asked

Pandiscia's lawyers have pleaded breach of implied contract, breach of express contract, unjust enrichment and unfair business practices. The suit seeks damages, restitution, disgorgement of the profits Amazon has drawn from AI products built partly on this data, and an injunction to stop the practice going forward. Neither Twitch nor Amazon has issued a public response to the scraping allegations themselves.

## Why a default setting matters so much

The legal fight is really about consent architecture, not just AI. Opt-out defaults are a well-worn tool in tech — most users never touch a settings menu, so whatever is pre-selected becomes the practical policy for the overwhelming majority of accounts. Minton's comment more or less conceded that point: an opt-in version of this feature would have starved Amazon's models of data, because almost nobody would have signed up voluntarily.

That is precisely the dynamic the plaintiffs want a court to treat as legally significant rather than just a design choice. If a platform can prove people didn't actively object, is that consent — or is it a workaround for consent that would never be freely given? Twitch is not the only company facing this question: YouTubers have brought a similar suit against Apple over alleged unauthorized scraping of video content for AI training, part of a widening docket of creator-versus-platform cases testing whether user-generated content can be repurposed for AI without separate payment.

## What's next

Amazon and Twitch have yet to respond formally in court, where the first real test will be whether Pandiscia's contract and unjust-enrichment theories survive an early motion to dismiss. A ruling in the streamers' favor would push platforms toward genuine opt-in consent and revenue-sharing for AI training data — a precedent that would ripple well beyond gaming, into any platform sitting on a trove of user-generated video, audio or text.

vaping-smoking-cessation-review.headline: Nicotine vapes remain the best route to quitting smoking, major review finds
vaping-smoking-cessation-review.body_md:
The Cochrane Collaboration, whose evidence reviews sit near the top of medicine's pecking order, has updated its living review of e-cigarettes as a smoking-cessation aid — and the conclusion, published on 25 August, is the strongest yet in vaping's favour. Regulated, nicotine-containing e-cigarettes now have what Cochrane rates as high-certainty evidence behind them: they help more smokers quit than nicotine patches or gum, the standard treatment offered on the NHS for the past three decades.[^1]

The scale of the effect is modest but real. Pooling 80 randomised controlled trials and 29,861 participants — nine of them added since the previous update — the reviewers, led by Dr Nicola Lindson at Oxford and Dr Jamie Hartmann-Boyce, now at the University of Massachusetts Amherst, found roughly four more successful quitters per 100 smokers using nicotine vapes compared with nicotine-replacement therapy, and about two more per 100 compared with non-nicotine e-cigarettes.[^2] "Quitting smoking is hard," Lindson said. "It's important that there are different options available." Hartmann-Boyce went further, calling regulated nicotine vapes "a proven and viable option" that is "substantially less harmful than smoking."[^2] Against behavioural support alone, or no help at all, the evidence is present but less certain — the trial designs there are thinner.

![A man using an e-cigarette](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/32/Vapor_From_An_E_Cig_User_-_Vape_Pen_-_Vaporizer_%2815818510247%29.jpg)

## A policy collision

The timing is awkward for Westminster. The Tobacco and Vapes Act received Royal Assent on 29 April, phasing in a rolling sales ban for anyone born on or after 1 January 2009 and tightening vape marketing generally.[^3] Ministers have simultaneously leaned on vaping as a quitting tool — NHS England's "Swap to Stop" scheme has handed out free starter kits to smokers since 2023 — while the Treasury prepares to make vaping markedly more expensive. A new Vaping Products Duty takes effect on 1 October, adding £2.20 per 10ml of e-liquid (£2.64 with VAT), and free distribution and vending-machine sales are banned from 29 October, ahead of a full advertising ban in June 2027.[^4] A review concluding that vapes are the single most effective route off cigarettes lands just as the products are becoming pricier and harder to give away — a contradiction public-health bodies and the vaping industry are both likely to press the Department of Health and Social Care to address.

Cochrane's caveats matter as much as its headline. The findings apply only to regulated, nicotine-containing devices bought through legitimate retailers — not the unlicensed disposables that flooded the UK market before June 2025's ban, which carry their own risks from unstable batteries and unverified e-liquid contents. Serious harms have not shown up in the trial data, but Cochrane notes that follow-up rarely extends beyond two years, so nothing here speaks to decades-long exposure. Cancer Research UK, which funds the ongoing review, continues to caution against vaping by anyone who has never smoked.[^2]

The next data point is less scientific than fiscal: whether the October duty measurably dents uptake of vaping as a cessation tool, a question the DHSC has yet to say it plans to monitor.

iberia-battery-storage-grid-strain.headline: Spain and Portugal battery-storage firms scramble as grid strain persists
iberia-battery-storage-grid-strain.body_md:
The blackout lasted less than a day. The reckoning has taken sixteen months and counting.

On 28 April 2025, the Iberian Peninsula lost roughly 15 gigawatts of generation — about 60% of Spanish demand at that moment — in the space of five seconds. Some 55 million people across Spain, Portugal and a sliver of southern France went dark for up to 23 hours. Trains stopped, hospitals switched to generators, card payments failed. Spain's National Commission on Markets and Competition later put the economic cost near $1.8 billion; more than 30 sanction proceedings against grid operator Red Eléctrica and other utilities are still open, with no final ruling on responsibility as of this month.

What the blackout exposed, more than any single cause, was how thin Spain's buffer had become. At the time, the country had installed roughly 25 megawatts of grid-scale battery storage — a rounding error next to the 6-7 gigawatts of pumped hydro it could call on, and dwarfed by the pace at which solar and wind capacity had been added. Sixteen months on, that mismatch hasn't closed. It has mutated into a scramble: battery developers racing for grid connections that don't exist yet, curtailed solar farms losing money in daylight, and two governments trying to build a market mechanism fast enough to matter.

## A market that grew 589% and is still not enough

Spain's battery fleet did expand fast after the blackout — installed BESS capacity rose from 28 megawatts in April 2025 to 193 megawatts a year later, according to Red Eléctrica figures, a 589% increase. Project applications in the connection pipeline grew even faster, up 464% year-on-year.

![Substation infrastructure of the kind now bottlenecking Spain's storage buildout](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/2/27/Miranda_de_Ebro_-_Subestaci%C3%B3n_el%C3%A9ctrica_2.jpg)

But 193 megawatts is still a fraction of the 22.5 gigawatts of storage Spain says it needs by 2030 under its national energy and climate plan, and it trails the roughly 500-megawatt target the country had originally set for 2025 alone. The UK, by comparison, already had 5.6 gigawatts of battery storage online before the Iberian blackout happened at all.

The constraint isn't appetite or capital. Red Eléctrica's registry shows accumulated connection requests now total 22.1 gigawatts — developers are asking. The problem is physical: substations and access points in the sunniest, most oversubscribed corners of the grid are saturated. An AFRY analysis cited by trade publication Energy-Storage.news found Spanish storage projects worth roughly €7 billion sitting in connection queues, representing about 40% of the national storage target — part of a wider European logjam in which some 455 gigawatts of battery projects across eight countries, including Spain, Britain, Germany and Italy, are stuck waiting on distribution-grid upgrades.

The practical result is curtailment: solar plants ordered to switch off because the wires can't carry what they generate. National curtailment is forecast at 3.05 terawatt-hours in 2026, roughly 2.5% of generation — but the average masks the real story. In Badajoz province, home to some of Extremadura's largest solar parks, curtailment has reached an average of 37% this year, according to an analysis by the Circe research centre, with the worst-affected connection nodes discharged as much as 22.5% of the time. Developers are advised to avoid any grid node running above 130% of rated saturation; large stretches of Extremadura and Aragón now exceed it.

## Utilities co-locate, optimisers chase megawatts

Faced with a queue rather than an open grid, the biggest players are building storage next to generation they already own rather than seeking fresh connections. Iberdrola, which has more than 56 gigawatts of renewables installed globally, has been pairing batteries with existing solar and wind sites to capture frequency response, balancing-market payments and day-ahead arbitrage from a single connection point — the company installed Spain's first battery at a renewables project at its Arañuelo photovoltaic plant in Cáceres and has since added storage at sites in Burgos and Huelva. In Portugal, EDP is building the 180-megawatt, 360-megawatt-hour BigBATT project at Carregado, part-funded by the EU Innovation Fund, and has paired battery storage with its Alqueva floating solar array in the Alentejo.

![Alcoutim solar demonstration platform in Portugal's Algarve, where hybrid PV and battery projects are being tested](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/8/81/Alcoutim_Solar_Platform.jpg)

A newer layer of the market — battery "optimisers" that trade flexibility on behalf of asset owners rather than build generation themselves — is growing fastest of all. Entrix, a German-founded flexibility trader, says it has passed 3 gigawatts and 8.5 gigawatt-hours of contracted battery capacity across Europe and expects 2 gigawatts operational by the end of this year, citing Iberian demand explicitly as a post-blackout tailwind; the firm raised €43 million in March to fund the expansion. Developers Prosolia and Grenergy have both advanced standalone storage projects in Spain and Portugal this year, betting that flexibility revenue — not subsidy — will carry the economics.

Portugal, meanwhile, is chasing its own version of the same race. Lisbon has committed €400 million to grid upgrades since the blackout and lifted its battery storage target toward 750 megawatts by early this year, rising to roughly 2 gigawatts by 2030, backed by a system-services auction. It had already awarded €113 million in incentives to 43 battery projects totalling 500 megawatts in the months before the blackout. Grid operator REN's queue and Red Eléctrica's are, functionally, two ends of the same bottleneck.

## Whether pricing alone can fix it

The deeper question — the one that will decide who makes money and who doesn't — is whether Spain's answer to the bottleneck is a market mechanism or a regulatory one. So far it has tried to make it a market mechanism. Since the blackout, Madrid has exempted battery flexibility from grid-access fees that still apply to consumption, opened voltage-control services to storage and renewables for the first time, and published new grid-access rules meant to route capacity toward projects that can actually connect, backed by a saturation map REE was due to publish in February. In late May, the European Commission approved a Spanish capacity market worth an estimated €9 billion over ten years, modelled loosely on Italy's MACSE scheme, which offers 15-year inflation-linked payments for firm capacity. Italy's first MACSE auction cleared in September 2025 four times oversubscribed, at around €52,000 per megawatt per year for four-hour storage — a data point Spanish investors are watching closely.

But Spain's own capacity auctions aren't expected to run until 2027, and developers still don't know the contracted volumes, price caps, or how much weight will go to new projects versus plants already operating. That gap — pricing signals approved in principle, not yet live in practice — is where the current scramble is happening: firms competing today for scarce connection slots under rules that won't be finalised for another year. If the queue clears faster than the market design catches up, competition and grid investment alone may be enough. If it doesn't, the pressure for Madrid or Brussels to intervene more directly — allocating connections by fiat rather than by price — will grow, and that would reshape who captures the returns from Iberia's storage build-out.

The next concrete marker is REE's saturation capacity map, meant to tell developers which nodes are actually worth bidding for, followed by the first details of Spain's capacity-market auction rules expected before the 2027 tender. Portugal's system-services auction outcome, still pending, will show whether Lisbon's more modest target is achievable on the current grid. Until one of those lands, the country with Europe's fastest-growing solar fleet will keep switching part of it off in the middle of the day.

tiktok-doj-privacy-settlement.headline: TikTok nears $400m settlement with DOJ over child-privacy violations
tiktok-doj-privacy-settlement.body_md:
TikTok is closing out one of its oldest legal headaches with one of its largest checks. The company and parent ByteDance have agreed to pay $400 million to resolve a Justice Department lawsuit accusing them of harvesting personal data from millions of children under 13 without parental consent — and then ignoring parents who asked for that data to be deleted.

The settlement, confirmed this week, closes a case the DOJ filed jointly with the Federal Trade Commission in August 2024. U.S. District Judge George H. Wu dismissed the underlying action with prejudice on 21 August, based on the parties' own stipulation. TikTok admits no wrongdoing.

![TikTok's former Culver City headquarters, at the centre of years of US regulatory scrutiny](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0b/TikTok_Headquarters.jpg)

## What the DOJ alleged

The complaint painted a picture of a platform that knew it had an underage-user problem and chose not to fix it. Investigators said TikTok let children sign up despite knowing their real ages, ran a dedicated "Kids Mode" that itself collected data without proper safeguards, and altered its registration flow in ways that made it harder to catch and remove young users — all while sitting under a standing legal obligation, dating to 2019, to prevent exactly this.

That obligation traces back to TikTok's predecessor, Musical.ly, which paid $5.7 million to the FTC in 2019 — at the time a record fine under the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) — and accepted a consent decree requiring it to police underage accounts going forward. The DOJ's case argued TikTok inherited that decree and broke it anyway.

## The mechanics of the payout

The $400 million splits into two pieces. TikTok pays $300 million immediately. The remaining $100 million is contingent: it falls due only once a court formally vacates the 2019 Musical.ly consent decree, which still carries its own reporting and monitoring obligations pending a hearing set for 21 September. Until then, TikTok remains under both the old decree and the terms of the new settlement — a belt-and-braces arrangement typical of how the DOJ has structured recent COPPA enforcement.

As part of the deal, TikTok has also committed to tighter age-verification controls and expanded tools letting parents see and manage what their children can access on the app.

## Context that's shifted since the case was filed

When the DOJ sued in 2024, TikTok's American operations still sat under a Chinese parent facing a legislated ban. That's no longer the picture. In January, ByteDance completed a restructuring that handed roughly 80% of a new US joint venture — TikTok USDS — to a consortium led by Oracle, Silver Lake and MGX, with ByteDance retaining a minority stake and no access to US user data. Oracle now acts as the venture's designated security auditor.

This settlement, in other words, resolves conduct from the pre-restructuring era rather than testing the new ownership structure. It's a legacy bill being paid down just as TikTok's US business tries to present itself as a clean, domestically supervised operation — one more item cleared off the ledger on the way to a fresh start.

## Why it doesn't move markets

TikTok isn't publicly traded, so there's no ticker to react and no earnings call where analysts will press on the number. For ByteDance — last valued in the hundreds of billions of dollars — $400 million is a rounding error, not a balance-sheet event. And unlike enforcement actions that hint at industry-wide crackdowns, this one is narrowly about TikTok's specific, well-documented history with underage users rather than a new legal theory that other platforms need to worry about.

What's worth watching instead is the 21 September hearing on the Musical.ly decree, and whether regulators use the newly restructured, Oracle-supervised TikTok as a test case for how seriously the new ownership takes compliance — the kind of scrutiny that, if it goes badly, would matter far more than a nine-figure fine ever could.

nfl-cte-study.headline: Study finds at least 25% of former NFL players had CTE brain disease
nfl-cte-study.body_md:
The finding itself reads like something out of a coroner's report, because in a sense it is: Mass General Brigham and Boston University researchers examined the brains of 878 former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021, and concluded that at least 24.5% of them had chronic traumatic encephalopathy. The real number, the researchers say, is probably a good deal higher — their upper-bound estimate reaches as high as 97.7%, though they caution that both extremes are unlikely and the truth sits somewhere in the wide territory between.

![Cross-sections comparing a normal brain with an advanced-stage CTE brain, showing shrinkage and ventricle enlargement](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/0/0c/Chronic_Traumatic_Encephalopathy.png)

The study, published this week in The BMJ, is a family affair for CTE research: it draws on the same Boston University brain bank that first put the disease on the map with Aaron Hernandez and Frank Gifford, among others. Of the 878 deceased players identified, 235 families donated brain tissue for examination — and of those, 215, or 91.4%, showed pathological signs of CTE. Extrapolating from a self-selected donor pool to the full former-player population is the statistical sleight of hand that produces both the study's headline number and its enormous uncertainty band; families are more likely to donate a brain when a player showed cognitive symptoms before death, which skews the sample toward more severe cases. The researchers built their 24.5% floor by assuming, conservatively, that every non-donating family's player was disease-free — a deliberately implausible assumption meant to establish a lower bound, not a best guess.

What isn't ambiguous is the severity among those who did test positive. More than 91% of the CTE-positive brains were classified as Stage IV, the most advanced form of the disease, and 61.3% of CTE cases met clinical criteria for dementia. Boston University's Ann McKee, the pathologist who has anchored this research for over a decade, called the findings a “wake-up call” in comments to the Boston Globe.

## Money follows the science

CTE research has moved from medical curiosity to financial liability with some regularity since the NFL's founding concussion settlement, and this study lands in the middle of an active legal and regulatory moment rather than a quiet one. The league's original 2015 settlement, which covers 65 years of claims, has now paid out more than $1.4 billion, but a Washington Post investigation this year found the NFL routinely uses medical loopholes to deny claims — precisely the kind of gap that a fresh, high-profile prevalence estimate tends to widen in court.

Sports betting operators have their own, more novel exposure. In March, the Public Health Advocacy Institute sued DraftKings, FanDuel, Genius Sports and the NFL jointly, arguing that microbetting and player-prop products are designed to be addictive — a case that ties the health of players' brains to the health of the products built to bet on them. DraftKings shares are already down roughly 50% over the past year on unrelated concerns about prediction-market competition eating into sportsbook volume; a jury verdict linking betting products to gambling harm, layered onto declining engagement, is not a scenario the market has fully priced.

## The ownership stakes have gotten bigger

The backdrop that makes all of this newly relevant to capital markets is that NFL teams themselves are now investable assets in a way they weren't a decade ago. Average franchise value hit roughly $9.3 billion this year, up 31%, and the league's 2024 decision to admit institutional capital has brought private equity firms — Arctos has stakes in the Buffalo Bills and Los Angeles Chargers, Sixth Street has a piece of the Patriots — directly onto team cap tables. Those investors are underwriting media-rights growth and stadium economics; a legal environment that reopens questions about the league's historical handling of brain injuries, or that produces a wave of new individual claims outside the settlement's release, sits on their balance sheets as a tail risk that valuation models rarely line-item explicitly.

## What to watch

The BMJ study itself changes no court docket today, but it arrives as ammunition for plaintiffs' lawyers ahead of ongoing claims disputes under the 2015 settlement and for the Pennsylvania betting-liability suit working through discovery. The next concrete marker is whether the NFL's settlement claims office, under continued Washington Post-style scrutiny, faces pressure from Congress or state attorneys general to loosen its medical criteria — a move that would raise the settlement's total cost and, by extension, the league's cash calls on owners carrying fresh private-equity partners.

pl-transfer-deadline-scramble.headline: Premier League clubs scramble before the 1 September transfer deadline
pl-transfer-deadline-scramble.body_md:
Nottingham Forest do not, as a rule, out-negotiate Chelsea for young English strikers. That they appear to have just done so — agreeing a club-record deal worth up to £50m for Liam Delap less than a week before the transfer window shuts — is the kind of detail that makes deadline week interesting beyond the usual scramble of loan swaps and medicals booked in airport hotels.

The deal, first reported by Fabrizio Romano and since confirmed by Sky Sports and ESPN, sees Forest pay around £45m up front with add-ons taking the total towards £50m. A medical is expected on Wednesday. For a club that finished seventh last season and whose entire summer has been shadowed by an ownership row between Evangelos Marinakis and outgoing manager Nuno Espírito Santo, it is a statement signing — the largest fee Forest have ever paid, for a player Chelsea signed just fourteen months ago.

## A striker nobody wanted enough

Delap's season at Stamford Bridge has been one of the summer's quieter disappointments. Signed from Ipswich Town for around £30m last year with real fanfare — an England-eligible number nine still only 22 — he managed just two goals in 41 appearances under Enzo Maresca and, more recently, Xabi Alonso, and was left out of the matchday squad entirely for Monday's 3-2 win over Fulham. Chelsea, mid-way through a wider squad clearout under Alonso, stand to turn a profit of roughly £20m on a player who barely got a run of games.

![Liam Delap warming up for Ipswich Town in December 2024, before his move to Chelsea](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/9/93/Wolves_v_Town%2C_Dec_2024_%2818%29_%28cropped%29.jpg)

That is precisely the kind of player mid-table clubs used to get on loan, not buy outright for a club record. Forest's own manager was notably circumspect when asked about it before Monday's game. "I can tell everybody that he doesn't play today," Oliver Glasner said. "Everything else we shall see in the next days." Romano's reporting suggests the deciding factor was more human than tactical: Delap, after speaking to Glasner directly, decided he would rather be first-choice at the City Ground than fighting for minutes in west London. Forest, who lost Taiwo Awoniyi to Coventry for £9m earlier in the window, needed a focal point up front — and were prepared to pay elite-level money to get one who is still young enough to improve.

## Arsenal's £128m gamble

The bigger number in this window belongs to Arsenal, who are pushing to sign Julián Álvarez from Atlético Madrid in a deal reportedly worth up to £128m — a British transfer record, if it lands. The 26-year-old Argentine had set his heart on Barcelona, but Atlético have refused to sell him to a direct La Liga rival, and Barcelona are understood to have told Álvarez they will not extend their own pursuit beyond this week. That leaves Arsenal as, in Sky Sports' phrase, "the only get-out" for a player who was reportedly left "devastated" by his own supporters' reaction to the saga.

![Julián Álvarez in Atlético Madrid colours during a Champions League match against Salzburg, January 2025](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/6/6f/Juli%C3%A1n_%C3%81lvarez%2C_FC_Salzburg_vs._Atletico_Madrid_%282025-01-29_UEFA_Championsleague%29_72_%28cropped%29.jpg)

Unlike Forest's move for Delap, this is not mid-table ambition outbidding tradition — it is the usual order reasserting itself, with the reigning Premier League champions using financial muscle to prise a wanted man from a club that would rather not sell him at all. Atlético are said to be holding firm on their €150m valuation, and ESPN describes the mood around the negotiation as "extremely tense" with barely a week of window left to resolve it.

## United's persistent itch

Manchester United, meanwhile, are still working the phones rather than signing contracts. A left-back has been on their list for weeks — Luke Shaw has started 43 of United's last 44 league matches, an underline of both his importance and the lack of any credible deputy — and Newcastle's Lewis Hall remains the preferred target. Newcastle, by most accounts, do not want to sell, which has pushed United to sound out alternatives including Barcelona's Alejandro Balde, whom they would rather take on loan than buy outright, and Racing Santander's Jorge Salinas. None of it, as of Wednesday, has produced an actual bid Newcastle would entertain. A new central midfielder remains on the same list, competing for the same finite transfer budget.

## What the week tells you

Three clubs, three different relationships with the market: Forest paying up for certainty, Arsenal paying up because the alternative is watching a rival sign a target they already wanted, and United still hoping a cheaper route to the same problem appears before Tuesday. The Delap fee is the one worth remembering after deadline day passes — not because £50m is enormous by modern standards, but because it was Nottingham Forest, not Manchester City or Arsenal, willing to pay it for a 22-year-old the traditional powers had already decided wasn't worth persisting with. Whether Glasner turns that gamble into goals will say more about the transfer window's real winners than any of the numbers being quoted this week.

The deadline falls at 11pm on 1 September. Delap's medical, Álvarez's fee negotiation with Atlético, and United's left-back search are all likely to resolve — one way or another — before then.
